collection: NERDC JSS 1 Mathematics counting in twos, binary numerals and fractions
note: Original classroom practice. Independent academic review pending.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Count complete groups of two and identify an unpaired item.
questions.prompt: Efe has 17 dry seed pods for a counting display. She puts two pods on each card until she cannot fill another card. How many cards are filled and how many pods are left?
questions.explanation: Counting 2, 4, …, 16 fills eight cards. One of the 17 pods is left.

verification.purpose: Account for the original number of pods.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Identify and repair an incorrect running count of pairs.
questions.prompt: A class records the total number of counters after each pair is placed on a tray: 2, 4, 6, 9, 10, 12. Which entry needs changing? Explain how the entries on either side help you check the change.
questions.answer: Replace 9 with 8. It is two more than 6 and two less than 10.
questions.explanation: The fourth pair gives eight counters. Checking both neighbouring totals confirms that every step adds two.

markingGuide.description: Checks the step from 6 to 8 and from 8 to 10.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.topic: Conversion of Base-ten numerals to Binary numbers
questions.learningObjective: Convert a decimal numeral to binary using division by two.
questions.prompt: Convert decimal 26 to binary by repeated division by two. Show the remainders and state the order in which you read them.
questions.answer: 11010 in base two. Read the remainders from last to first.
questions.explanation: The successive quotients are 13, 6, 3, 1, 0 and the remainders are 0, 1, 0, 1, 1. Reading upward gives 11010, worth 16 + 8 + 2 = 26.

markingGuide.description: Shows successive division by two with the correct quotients and remainders.
States that the last remainder is read first.

verification.purpose: Check the place values of the converted binary numeral.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.topic: Conversion of Base-ten numerals to Binary numbers
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the final-bit pattern in consecutive binary numerals.
questions.prompt: A board shows consecutive counts in binary: 1000, 1001, 1010, 1011, 1100. How does the rightmost digit change as the count increases by one?
questions.explanation: The rightmost place is the ones place. All the places to its left have even values, so the rightmost digit is 0 for an even count and 1 for an odd count.
options: It stays at 0 until all the other digits change.
It changes only when the leftmost digit changes.
It stays at 1 once it has reached 1.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.topic: Conversion of Base-ten numerals to Binary numbers
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a short bit string as a record of on and off states.
questions.prompt: Four indicator lamps are listed from left to right. The controller records a 1 for a lit lamp and a 0 for an unlit lamp. The record is 0101. Which lamps are lit?
questions.explanation: The digits correspond to the lamps in their listed order. The two 1s are in positions two and four.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Determine a missing denominator in an equivalent fraction.
questions.prompt: A pattern uses blue thread for 5/12 of its stitches. On a chart with 15 blue stitches, how many total stitches would keep exactly the same fraction blue?
questions.explanation: The blue count is tripled from 5 to 15. Tripling the total from 12 to 36 preserves the fraction.

verification.purpose: Check that the blue fractions are equivalent.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Order fractions that describe equal-sized wholes.
questions.prompt: Three teams receive identical strips of cloth. They use 7/12, 5/8 and 2/3 of their strips. List the fractions from least cloth used to most. Use a common denominator to justify your order.
questions.explanation: Because the strips have the same length, comparing their fractions directly is valid. Expressing them in twenty-fourths makes the comparison 14 < 15 < 16.

markingGuide.description: Writes all three equivalent fractions with a common denominator.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.subtopic: Decimal to fraction in lowest terms
questions.learningObjective: Convert a terminating decimal to a reduced fraction using place value.
questions.prompt: A gauge shows that a container is 0.36 full. A pupil writes 36/10. Use place value to correct the denominator, then give the fraction in lowest terms.
questions.explanation: The last digit of 0.36 is in the hundredths place, so the unreduced fraction is 36/100. Divide both terms by four.

markingGuide.description: Explains that 0.36 has 36 hundredths and writes 36/100.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Express a fraction as a percentage including a half-percent.
questions.prompt: A club repairs three of the eight identical shelves on its work list. What percentage of its shelves has it repaired?
questions.explanation: Each eighth is 100% ÷ 8 = 12.5%. Three eighths are 37.5%.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a percentage as a reduced fraction of a whole.
questions.prompt: A library sets aside 85% of its display space for pupils’ work. What fraction of the entire display space does this represent in lowest terms?
questions.explanation: Eighty-five percent is 85 out of 100. Dividing both terms by five gives 17/20.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.subtopic: Equivalent shares of a common fund
questions.learningObjective: Use equivalent fractions to compare two shares of the same amount.
questions.prompt: Two activity teams get 4/10 and 6/15 of the same ₦15,000 fund respectively. Do their shares have equal value? Show how the fractions tell you and calculate the value of each share.
questions.answer: Yes. Both fractions simplify to 2/5, so each team receives ₦6,000.
questions.explanation: Divide 4 and 10 by two and 6 and 15 by three. Both fractions become 2/5. One fifth of ₦15,000 is ₦3,000, so two fifths are ₦6,000.

markingGuide.description: Shows that 4/10 and 6/15 both equal 2/5 or gives another valid equivalence proof.
Concludes that the two shares have equal value.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.learningObjective: Find a whole quantity from a known fractional part.
questions.prompt: At the end of a shift, 21 finished badges represent seven ninths of the planned output. How many badges must the next shift finish to meet the plan? Show how you find the number of badges represented by one ninth.
questions.explanation: Seven ninths represent 21 badges, so one ninth represents 21 ÷ 7 = 3 badges. Two ninths remain, which is six badges.

verification.purpose: Check the number of badges remaining.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.subtopic: Fraction to decimal on a scale
questions.learningObjective: Convert a fraction to the decimal notation used on a scale.
questions.prompt: A scale from 0 to 1 metre has labels at intervals of 0.05 m. A peg is 11/20 m from the zero mark. What decimal label is beside the peg?
questions.explanation: Multiplying numerator and denominator by five gives 55/100 m, or 0.55 m.
